## 2026-11-19 xredis Cluster primary loss and promotion

An accepted transport disconnect invalidates the route's map generation and
preserves the native result and delivery certainty. A refused first primary
admission against an empty, disconnected maintained pool can request one
fresh map before sending any business bytes. Ordinary capacity overload keeps
its existing wait and overload contract. The pool retains observed transport
loss through failed replacement construction and clears it on new readiness.

An initial real Redis 8.0.5 run exposed SHARDS replies that retained the dead
master beside the promoted online master. The corrected parser recognizes
`fail` and `failed`, retains predecessor records and selects a unique online
owner. Multiple online masters and ambiguous health combinations still reject
atomically. RESP2 and RESP3 parser tests cover both record orders.

Three owned loopback Cluster trials killed the original primary during two
server-observed BLPOP operations. Three primary shards and one replica ran
under WSL. Windows and WSL native clients exercised the RESP3/SHARDS
disconnected path and the RESP2/SLOTS unsent path. In-flight outcomes stayed
DISCONNECTED/MAY_HAVE_EXECUTED with one native attempt. The other clients
still held the pre-election map and recovered on their first post-election
write. Every probe obtained one successful INCR on the promoted primary
without MOVED or manual invalidation. The four counters each reached one
in every trial. The promoted endpoint used a new ordinary pool distinct from
its prewarmed replica pool.

| Loopback observation | Range across the three trials |
| --- | ---: |
| Process kill to survivor slot agreement | 1.968–2.775 s |

## 2026-11-19 xredis unsent calls across a Cluster election

The previous mainline build reproduced a terminal NO_ROUTE after the first
refresh still reported the unavailable owner. The real Redis candidate still
reported itself as a replica when the test submitted the write.

The client now keeps the unsent operation in its existing map wait queue after
a confirmed primary outage. For that operation, it coalesces up to
`1 + Route.MaxWaits` map waits under the original deadline. Unconfirmed missing
slots retain the single refresh. Native pool waits remain cumulative across
maps. The code keeps the original charge and command storage while waiting.
When a new endpoint fits the existing route, the controller rebinds it in
place. A larger endpoint can allocate a replacement within the same admission
reservation. Native attempts that were already accepted retain their
existing outcome and delivery rules.

Scripted peers verify exhaustion of the map budget, cancellation and deadline
while metadata is held, and one native attempt after a new owner appears.
The single-header probe exercises unchanged-map reuse in a one-byte allocation
budget and injected failure when a larger endpoint requires a new allocation.
Both branches preserve the original deadline and command bytes.
A separate progress-engine barrier reproduces a queued call missing an
already published generation. The worker now uses that generation without
waiting for another refresh notification.

Three Redis 8.0.5 loopback elections each included a Windows and a WSL
client submitting a write before the candidate promoted. The driver
independently checked the replica role after observing both submissions.
The six writes observed 31–44 metadata refresh starts per client at a 100 ms
minimum refresh interval. Each made a single native attempt on the promoted
primary and left a server counter of one. The in-flight disconnect and
post-election write cases also passed in each trial.

## 2026-11-19 xrpc Duplex deadline index

The owner indexes one finite deadline per outgoing operation, including batches
and notifications. Info reads the minimum in constant time. The existing
MaxWork budget covers due operations and cancellation work. The rotating
raw-token cancellation cohort preserves its membership boundary while
operations are added or removed. The native producer still determines exact timeout,
cancellation and delivery status.

The regression holds a 128-call window, retires both the minimum and a
nonminimum by reply, and adds a near deadline at the tail. With MaxWork=1
the old Duplex translation unit fails the two-owner-turn completion check
on both platforms. The indexed implementation passes, including raw token
cancellation and complete retirement.

Measured with GCC O2 against 400d85e4. Each cell is the median of seven paired
runs after one warmup. The p99 is taken over blocks of 64 Info queries.

## 2026-11-19 xrpc host-driven framed stdio

The new stdio module binds a frame configuration and the existing Duplex
endpoint to two host-provided nonblocking byte callbacks. Content-Length and
UINT32_BE remain explicit. The adapter bounds read storage, write offers
and owner work, retains one overloaded frame and preserves its incoming
deadline through retry.

Clean EOF drains accepted handler responses. It retires unstarted outgoing
calls and preserves the framing boundary of any started output while the
drain budget permits. An EOF deadline regression exposes the previous
candidate writing after a zero drain budget when the peer becomes writable
during EOF observation. The fixed candidate checks the budget before another
write. The tests also cover raw output pressure, cancellation after partial
write, malformed and truncated input, I/O contracts and allocation rollback.

The Windows and WSL aggregates each verified 59 existing programs and two
added stdio programs. Separate stdio suites, WSL ASan/UBSan with leak checks,
two trim probes and all eight root/leaf static/shared consumers passed.
The independent Python peer verifies both formats over real redirected pipes
while the stream is open and through EOF. A 32 KiB result is consumed after a
delayed read. Both single-object dependency inspections found zero forbidden
network, TLS, HTTP, WebSocket or process symbols.

## 2026-11-19 native process pipes for the xrpc owner

Windows CreatePipe completed a ReadFile with an OVERLAPPED argument only
after the probe writer supplied one byte 125 ms later. The Process pipe
leaf now provisions distinct native endpoints for the existing public
Process launcher. The child keeps ordinary blocking stdin/stdout. The
parent waits for I/O or a concurrent wake with an explicit deadline.
Windows uses one bounded staging buffer per direction and cancels and joins
pending operations on close. POSIX uses a nonblocking process input socket
and stdout pipe, reading and writing directly through the offered spans.
The leaf uses the existing Process waiter and adds no thread.

The modular, single-header and example programs passed on Windows GCC,
Windows TinyCC and WSL GCC. The WSL example and tests also passed ASan,
UBSan and leak checking. The native peer echoed 1 MiB through input
half-close and output EOF. The tests cover an unread child, pending Windows
retirement, independent process lifetime, child death, constructor OOM and
recovery, Linux fd exhaustion during setup and native handle count
stability after failed launches. The six-program Process/I/O regression
passed per platform. Four independent declaration consumers exchanged data
over Windows and WSL static/shared packages.

The portable xrpc adapter remains the next consumer. Native Linux and
sustained qualification remain open.

## 2026-11-19 stdio write completion before response dispatch

A deterministic host fixture made the final write retry return AGAIN at
the start of an owner turn, then made the complete reply readable and the
write completion observable. The previous stdio loop would keep the write
lane paused and dispatch the reply while the request still appeared
partially sent. The regression failed on the prior Windows build.

Assembling a frame now permits one retry of the started write before
dispatch. The extra retry is bounded by completed frame assembly and
preserves the existing per-turn progress budget. Windows and WSL
modular/single-header tests passed in both framing profiles. The initial
failure and both passing builds are in
out/service-extensions/xrpc-stdio-process-20261119/stdio-order-*.log.

## 2026-11-19 xrpc native subprocess stdio

The stdio process leaf launches an ordinary blocking subprocess through the
existing XRT process pipes. The host owns each bounded Step and Wait. Wait
combines native read/write readiness, cross-thread signals, cached RPC
deadlines and the caller's earlier wait budget. At a terminal protocol
snapshot the adapter closes child stdin and retires any pending native
write. Destroy requires the duplex state to be drained and then retires
remaining native I/O. The process reference and typed call results have
independent lifetimes.

Windows and WSL each passed 63 aggregate programs and 30 examples. The
final focused suite on each platform also verifies retirement while an
executing handler still holds an endpoint reference. It passed under WSL
ASan/UBSan with leak detection. The focused modular TSan run passed
with GCC's existing warning that atomic_thread_fence is uninstrumented.
The xrpc root and subprocess-leaf consumers used real static and shared
packages on both platforms. The independent Python peer and the
existing host-driven child examples passed both framing profiles. Single
objects for both stdio leaves found zero forbidden symbols.

## 2026-11-19 xrpc negotiated deadlines

Duplex and framed stdio negotiate deadline propagation per direction. A
selected finite document carries the remaining caller budget in the same
charged wire allocation. The receiver uses its own monotonic clock and
its configured limit. Framed input starts that clock at the first
fragment. Expiry bypasses further business and produces bounded errors
for the original call IDs. A mixed batch keeps one deadline and one
response shape. The connection can carry more work after expiry.

Windows and WSL each passed 63 aggregate and six selected test programs.
The selected runs cover modular and single-header builds, fragmented
arrival and both native subprocess framing profiles. The duplex example
and eight static/shared package consumers return the remote deadline
error and continue using the connection. WSL ASan/UBSan with leak checks
and focused TSan passed. GCC leaves atomic_thread_fence uninstrumented
under TSan. Three single-object variants contain no forbidden symbols
on either platform. The strict gate still lists the same 20 developing
xrpc modules.

## 2026-11-19 xcron compensation at forward transitions

An opt-in recurring-job policy runs once at a forward offset transition
when the gap contains a matching nominal time with zero global UTC
candidates. The service delivers the earliest missing label with the
transition as the scheduled instant. Additional missing matches and an
actual match at the same instant coalesce into the same delivery.

The selected-service batch test executes two eligible jobs and verifies
the local label on each callback and receipt. A file-backed checkpoint
group is committed and reopened before the transition. The restored job
executes on schedule. A second commit and reopen verifies that the
exhausted job retains one recorded success and does not replay.
Checkpoint readers must be upgraded before writing the new policy.

Tests ran from D:/GIT/xrt master on Windows and Ubuntu in WSL.
Each host ran 21 modular and 25 single-header programs, two package
consumers for static and shared builds, and the occurrence example.
Windows skipped two symlink fixtures with system error 1314.
WSL occurrence and checkpoint tests passed ASan/UBSan with leak checking.
Selected-service and checkpoint tests passed TSan. GCC's standalone atomic
fence is outside that instrumentation.

The independent tzdb 2026e oracle ran 195,416 queries per host across
422 zones, with 3,808 compensated results. Per-zone results matched on
both hosts. The oracle checks both synchronous forms and every bounded
cursor step, including forward transitions from history and footer rules
and inclusive and exclusive queries at the transition.

| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Windows | Compensate, synchronous | 1,258,981 | 39.2 | 45.4 |
| Windows | Compensate, cursor budget 1 | 981,347 | 52.3 | 57.7 |
| WSL | Compensate, synchronous | 1,242,075 | 48.1 | 99.0 |
| WSL | Compensate, cursor budget 1 | 954,323 | 59.6 | 112.7 |

The table uses medians of nine pinned runs with 320,000 queries per run
and 32 queries per timed batch. Both runs exceeded the existing sample
variability limits. The cursor completed the fixture in four steps per
query. The reports preserve unpinned and pinned measurements.

The same-harness control compared the previous and current builds with

folded case had a +11.5% paired P99.9 change. The 12-pair pinned follow-up

## 2026-11-19 Managed Cluster command catalogue

The optional catalogue cache fetches a full COMMAND response from a
caller-selected authorized primary. A control caller validates it and
publishes it before the original deadline. Concurrent refresh returns
BUSY, and prior valid snapshots survive failures. Explicit invalidation
fences an in-flight response. Close seals publication. Cached calls
take a retained snapshot before existing immutable key evaluation and
admission. The caller chooses when to refresh.

Windows and WSL passed the cache, command-key and synchronous Cluster
programs, the standalone cache fixture and example, and separate static
and shared package consumers. The cache fixture covers ACL refusal,
malformed metadata, limits, allocation and wait failure, stale
replacement, a late timeout reply and close. WSL ASan/UBSan with leak
checking and Clang TSan passed.

Redis 8.0.5 exercised all 36 native cases per host with full COMMAND
and cached INCR, using numeric, DNS and prepared endpoints. RESP2,
RESP3 and AUTO were covered with SHARDS/SLOTS and actual ASK/MOVED.
Four producers verified each distinct integer from 1 to 32 and the final
server value in every case. The harness joined all owned nodes.

The endpoint now accepts complete JSON-RPC documents from the host. The host
can dispatch on its own executor and complete a bounded incoming request on

cancellation and uncertain-result handling. The in-memory and stdio examples
demonstrate application-owned dispatch. Transport, framing, process supervision
and the application executor have left the library. The previous implementations
and paused trim patch remain available at befcce75 and in the local proof directory,

matches and dollar-prefixed topic rules. A destination matching several filters
receives one copy if any of them permits the delivery. Sixteen keyed shards
index first-literal filters and one shard indexes leading wildcards. Shared
read locks let publishers traverse the same shard concurrently. Filter
updates and connection retirement take the corresponding write lock.

## 2026-11-19 MQTT QoS 0 retained messages and subscription options

The server retains the latest QoS 0 publication per topic within topic and
byte quotas. An empty retained publication clears the old entry and can still
reach live subscribers. The broker reclaims due records on retained writes.
Exact and wildcard ordinary subscriptions can replay retained messages with
expiry adjustment. MQTT 5 Retain Handling, Retain As Published and No Local
govern replay and live forwarding. Shared subscriptions only receive live
publications. Retained state and publisher identities stay in memory.

The initial 64-peer benchmark timed out after some SUBACKs because custom
xmap key callbacks change a shared reentry flag during lookup. Concurrent
readers could miss an existing topic. Both exact routing and retained lookup
now use the existing intrusive AVL index, ordered by keyed hash and then
topic bytes, under the shard's read/write lock. Retention has its own shards'
locks. The fixed build delivered every response in the standalone 64-peer
reproduction, 512 rounds on each host. A separate versioned 64-peer test
also checks 2,048 successful replays in the mixed-version peer suite.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed both protocol selections, modular and
single-header builds, native static and shared consumers, dependency trims
and the independent Python peer. Tests exercise wire expiry and reclamation,
quota and allocation rollback, same-Client-ID replay suppression across

## 2026-11-19 MQTT server bidirectional QoS 1

MQTT 5 and 3.1.1 subscribers can receive QoS 1. A request for QoS 2 receives
QoS 1. Delivery respects source QoS and the highest matching subscription
grant for the same retained-flag variant. Shared groups and retained replays
use the same outgoing delivery path. The destination's worker owns the pending
FIFO and active identifiers. PUBACK, including an MQTT 5 negative reason,
releases protocol credit. Native buffer release independently retires the
shared payload reference. Each recipient copies only the packet prefix it
needs to patch. The broker charges the full packet size against its byte quota.

The broker enforces the subscriber's Receive Maximum and negotiated packet
size. TCP backpressure keeps the pending message until drain. Expired waiting
messages retire without starting a send. Fresh sends adjust the expiry property
without changing User Property order. Exhaustion terminates the affected clean
session, with DISCONNECT 0x97 attempted on MQTT 5. Control replies can proceed
while the PUBLISH window is full.

## 2026-11-19 MQTT server session ownership and takeover

An authorized CONNECT constructs one session with its Client ID in the same
allocation. The registry and topic links point to that session. It owns the
subscription list, QoS 1/2 indexes, outbound FIFO and identifier allocator.
The peer owns its stream, endpoint limits and connection timers. Native send
references still pin the bound peer through this stage. Topic shards keep
linked sessions alive through routing and retirement.

A Client ID takeover makes the prior session unavailable under the identity
registry gate. Native close runs after that gate is released, with a peer
reference held through the abort request. Ordinary and shared routing skip
obsolete links while the prior worker retires. The session allocation failure
path leaves the established session reachable. The race check exposed an early
publication of the transport packet limit through the registry. The limit is
now initialized before the session is registered.

The new socket fixture accepts two streams on separate workers, holds the old
worker with its ordinary and shared links still indexed and checks that the new
connection can take over. A QoS 1 publication targeting those links receives
No Matching Subscribers. The first version of the fixture blocked listener
accept as well. The final fixture accepts both TCP streams before holding the
old worker. The single-header suite also injects a session allocation failure
and verifies that the previous owner still responds.

session lifetime. The broker keeps subscriptions, inbound QoS 2 duplicate

`MaxPersistentSessions` caps retained session count. Outgoing count and wire
byte budgets cover offline queues and continuing exchanges. Offline ordinary
subscriptions admit QoS 1/2. Shared selection uses online members. Resource
exhaustion seals the affected session. Expiry and shutdown release retained

their position in the bounded offline queue while shared routing skips
the detaching peer. One successor can reserve the saved session. If that
connection aborts or times out, the broker can return eligible state to its
expiry list. A clean replacement continues to seal the old state immediately.

## 2026-11-19 MQTT Clean Start takeover ordering

A live Client ID replacement that creates fresh state now reserves the new
session, seals the old state and pauses the successor's reads. The old
worker sends the MQTT 5 takeover notification when its transport admits it.
After the old transport and subscriptions retire, the successor can send
CONNACK with Session Present clear and begin processing control packets.
A competing claimant receives Server Busy while the reservation is pending.
Allocation failure happens before replacement and leaves the prior
connection usable. A canceled clean successor retires its reservation.
The previous state stays sealed once its takeover starts.

The held-worker fixture tests both acceptance and cancellation, checks that
old wildcard and shared links accept no new deliveries while they retire,
and confirms that the new CONNACK waits for physical retirement. A later
CONNECT after cancellation starts with an empty session. Windows x64 and
Ubuntu/WSL x64 ran the MQTT 5-only and dual-version modular and single-header
suites and separate Python peer checks. WSL passed ASan/UBSan with leak
checking and the full single-header TSan test. Generated headers and API
checks passed. Evidence is under
out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-clean-takeover-*.

Will publication and cancellation, durable recovery, transport variants and
the native Linux and long-duration performance gates remain open.

## 2026-11-19 MQTT server in-memory Wills

The broker admits version 5 and 3.1.1 Wills through CONNECT and topic
authorization. It owns a canonical PUBLISH and the Client ID in one
allocation. MaxWillBytes defaults to 16 MiB and limits live and detached
records. WillBytes exposes the charge. MQTT 5 refuses quota excess with
0x97 and allocation failure with 0x88. A refused or unaccepted CONNECT
does not arm its Will.

Normal DISCONNECT disarms the record. Network closure and MQTT 5 reason
0x04 release it after the earlier of Will Delay and Session Expiry.
An eligible resume cancels a still-pending Will, and Clean Start ends
the old session and publishes its pending Will. The expiry sweep and
old-transport retirement each detach the owned records before routing
outside the registry lock. Publication reuses the broker's existing
routing, retention and offline QoS path. Message Expiry starts when the
Will becomes a publication. Shutdown releases pending volatile Wills.
The configuration and information structures each gained one field.

The socket suite covers clean and abnormal closure, 0x04, Will Delay,
earlier session expiry, duration of Message Expiry, live and offline
resume, Clean Start against live and offline state, retained QoS 1,
offline QoS 1, topic admission, OOM and storage quota. The separate Python
peer verifies normal suppression and abnormal publication for MQTT 5 and
3.1.1 over the native listener. Both hosts passed MQTT 5-only and dual-version
modular and single-header builds and static and shared package consumers.
The first ASan single-header run exposed a test assumption about the order
in which two accept callbacks were registered. The fixture now completes
the publisher's CONNECT before dialing the old session. The final WSL

checks passed. The codec-only text size stayed fixed. Compared with

and 2,747 on WSL across the Clean Start and Will changes.

## 2026-11-19 MQTT expiry under native timer pressure

The fault fixture configures two timer credits on each of two workers.
After CONNACK it fills every credit still available, closes the publisher
and waits for its one-second Will Delay and two-second Session Expiry.
Before the fix the Will receive timed out with no other traffic to trigger
expiry scheduling.

The broker now reserves its first expiry sweep before admitting the first
persistent session. Core commit a1c4146e adds xrtNetEngineEvery, which keeps
the same timer ID, node and worker credit across ticks. The initial timer
ceiling returns Server Busy before committing a session. The broker uses one
credit until shutdown and wakes once a second after first persistent use,
including when the offline list is empty. No allocation or queue command is
needed to schedule the next sweep. The one-shot node's heap index fits in
32 bits under TimerLimit. Packing the period next to that index preserved the
64-byte node cache class. An earlier layout exceeded the class and failed
the existing cached-timer OOM test.

The first regression fixture verifies Will Delay, Will publication, memory
credit return and actual session expiry with both workers still saturated.
The admission fixture leaves a single credit per worker, verifies refusal
before persistent state is installed, then connects without persistence.
A third fixture fills the expiry worker's command queue during Close and
checks the ticker retires on its own worker. The core tests cover repeated
triggers with the only credit held, self-cancellation, reuse and shutdown.

the MQTT 5-only and dual-version modular and single-header broker suites,
the static and shared package consumers, and the independent Python peer.

## 2026-11-19 MQTT broker TLS transport

The selectable xmqtt_server_tls module attaches a new accepted TCP stream
through XRT TLS. Application TLS policy and credentials supply the listener's
identity. The CONNECT deadline covers TLS handshake time. The shared MQTT
parser pulls up only a complete fragmented record when needed and asks TLS
for more plaintext when a prefix is incomplete. Session identity, admission,
routing, Wills, quotas and QoS continue through the existing broker path.

A per-peer plaintext FIFO charges wire bytes and record metadata to the native
write limit, with independent XRT ciphertext limits. Cross-worker publication
retains wire references through encryption. Control packets are copied to their
queue record. The owning worker drains at most the previously queued charge
per dispatch and retries only the unwritten suffix after a short write. Graceful
close drains the FIFO before TLS shutdown. Abort discards queued references,
and takeover waits for TLS and TCP physical retirement. The TLS-only
dependencies enable AES, SHA-256 and X25519 for the runnable TLS 1.3 example.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed TCP-only broker regressions and
dependency trims, TLS static and shared package consumers, and certificate-
verifying Python peers against both modular and single-header TLS listeners.
The independent probe covers MQTT 5 and 3.1.1, fragmented CONNECT and

authenticated closure and 48 queued QoS 1 deliveries read back in order.
The same probe passed on WSL under ASan/UBSan with leak checking and TSan.

One TLS 1.3 loopback connection ran one warm-up and three 1,000-request PING

## 2026-11-19 MQTT broker WS and WSS handoff

Selectable WS and WSS modules take the native transport on its worker after
HTTP Upgrade. The call hands XRT the header prefix to consume and preserves
the suffix. The common broker parser handles binary frames as a byte stream.
It reads complete packets from the current decoded span and stages partial
packets or a paused takeover suffix under the MQTT packet cap. A non-binary
data message schedules WebSocket close 1003.

The broker shares the bounded worker-owned output queue with direct TLS.
WS transfers single immutable references to XRT and joins reliable prefix
and payload when one frame needs both. Close drains queued data and worker
retirement waits for the physical WebSocket and transport tails. The loopback
APP example validates the mqtt subprotocol on /mqtt, supplies optional TLS
credentials and bounds pending Upgrade count and time.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed TCP broker regressions, direct TLS
interop and both WS/WSS static and shared package consumers. The independent
peer passed against modular and single-header samples for WS and WSS. It
checks exactly negotiated mqtt, rejects a missing mqtt offer and text data,
pipelines a WebSocket suffix at Upgrade, splits MQTT across continuations
and distinct messages, coalesces packets, verifies bidirectional QoS 1/2,
replays an active takeover and reads 48 queued QoS deliveries in order.
The same test waits for an unfinished Upgrade to retire during sample
shutdown. It passed WSL ASan/UBSan with leak checking and TSan.
Generated headers and API checks passed.

Each modular sample ran one warm-up and three 1,000-request sequential
PING runs on an established connection. Measurements include Python peer
processing. Throughput and P99 are the medians of the three runs.

| Host | Transport | PINGs/s | P99 (us) |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Windows x64 | WS | 22,074 | 74.0 |
| Windows x64 | WSS | 15,019 | 104.5 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | WS | 12,717 | 123.3 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | WSS | 9,895 | 174.0 |

Raw evidence is under out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-ws-*.

## 2026-11-19 MQTT 5 broker enhanced authentication

The selectable server auth module handles initial CONNECT/AUTH exchanges and
online reauthentication on the broker's existing connection worker. An APP
step supplies proof decisions and data. Its release callback retires exchange
state on completion, denial, timeout, peer close and broker shutdown.
The broker bounds exchange bytes, challenge rounds and time. It builds the
successful initial CONNACK before claiming the Client ID, then sets Session
Present when the session handoff completes. An online exchange has its own
deadline and existing traffic continues under the prior authority. Ordinary
broker connections allocate no enhanced authentication state.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed the MQTT TCP regression suite, auth
allocation and bounds tests, and static and shared auth package consumers.
On both environments an independent Python peer verified two HMAC challenge
rounds and the final proof against modular and single-header examples. It
covered in-flight QoS 1 traffic during reauthentication, failed and successful
Client ID takeover, method and reason validation, byte and round quotas,
CONNECT and reauthentication deadlines, and shutdown with an active
exchange. WSL ASan/UBSan with leak detection and TSan passed the socket
probe and the authentication whitebox tests. API coverage reports no missing
entries. Raw evidence is under
out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-auth-*.

The auth socket probe used TCP. Combined auth with TLS and WebSocket, durable
broker recovery, native Linux, controlled performance comparisons and
72-hour mixed loads remain open. Strict release reports 41 developing
modules.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT broker retained checkpoint recovery

The optional broker store module visits retained publications after close and
drain, before destruction. Each borrowed record includes the source wire and
version, publisher ID and remaining lifetime. Restore validates the complete
set and copies it into a new broker before attachment. It deducts downtime,
enforces existing retained quotas and rolls back all copies on a failed
record. The normal replay path preserves MQTT 5 No Local and recodes
retained messages for a different protocol version.

The loopback APP example owns the versioned file format, CRC, UTC check and
atomic replacement. An independent Python peer captured retained QoS 1 and
MQTT 3.1.1 messages, restarted the broker twice, and verified the newest
binary payload, publisher suppression, cross-version replay, expiry during
downtime and an already cleared topic. It also verified that truncated,
corrupt and future-dated files prevent startup and remain intact.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed modular and single-header restart
probes, MQTT TCP regressions, and static and shared package consumers. The
offline recovery tests covered wire and expiry validation, duplicate keys,
byte limits and OOM rollback. On WSL, these tests and the restart probe
passed ASan/UBSan with leak checking and TSan. The shared listener also
passed enhanced authentication over TCP, TLS, WS and WSS on both hosts.
Generated files and API coverage passed. Raw evidence is under
out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-retained-restart-*.

Broker session and Will recovery, durable acknowledgment ordering on
unexpected restart, native Linux, controlled performance comparisons and
72-hour mixed loads remain open. Strict release reports 42 developing
modules.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT broker session checkpoints

Close for checkpoint seals admission and drains native owners while
preserving persistent sessions. The owner visits records with one monotonic
cut for session state. Restore rebuilds existing indexes and quotas before
attachment. It keeps subscription options, incoming QoS 2 deduplication,
unsent FIFO order, sent identifiers and acknowledgment phases, and already
scheduled delayed Wills. Failed restore retires the provisional sessions.
The APP file example saves these records alongside retained messages and
loads its previous retained-only format.

An independent peer restarted MQTT 5 and 3.1.1 sessions in another process.
It verified QoS 1 DUP with the original packet identifier, QoS 2 PUBREL
continuation, incoming QoS 2 duplicate suppression, offline delivery through
the recovered wildcard subscription, and publication of a delayed Will that
became due during downtime. The suite included a still-connected persistent
client at the shutdown boundary. Recovery unit tests covered expired session
removal, duplicate identifier rejection, quota accounting and OOM rollback.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed modular and single-header restart
probes, TCP broker regression tests, and static and shared package consumers.
WSL ASan/UBSan with leak checking and TSan passed the recovery tests and
independent peer probe. Generated headers and API coverage checks passed.
Raw evidence is under
out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-session-checkpoint-*.

Live store commits before protocol acknowledgments for unexpected restart,
native Linux, controlled performance comparisons and 72-hour mixed loads
remain open.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT live retained commit

The selectable backend interface reserves the retained index and budget
before submitting a publication or tombstone to the APP. The asynchronous
ticket holds an immutable PUBLISH and retires on its connection worker.
Confirmed commit applies the retained state before publication and PUBACK
or PUBREC. Known failure preserves the prior version. Unknown outcome seals
admission and requires recovery from the authoritative backend. One pending
ticket holds a retained shard and pauses its publishing peer while other
peers keep operating.

The APP example owns a single retained topic slot, a bounded XRT task pool,
the file format and atomic file replacement. The independent TCP peer
terminated fresh broker processes before and after commits. It checked
restart of successful QoS 1/2 and 3.1.1 writes, interrupted replacement,
committed deletion, pending writes during shutdown, and admission sealing
after a write failure. TLS, WS and WSS probes exercised QoS 0 and QoS 1
and verified that coalesced PING packets remained ordered across the pause.
The unit test covered precommit invisibility, overlapping shard admission,
OOM and quota rollback.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed the modular and single-header probes,
TCP regressions, and static and shared package consumers. WSL ASan/UBSan
with leak checking and TSan passed the commit unit and independent probes.
Raw evidence is under
out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-retained-live-*.

This path persists retained client PUBLISH packets. Online recipient
session state, QoS 2 duplicate suppression and retained Wills still need
durable integration. Retained Wills are refused while the backend is enabled.
Strict release reports 43 developing modules. Native Linux, controlled
performance comparisons and 72-hour mixed loads remain open.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT durable retained Wills

A fired retained Will now uses the existing APP commit ticket. Its
immutable record keeps the original client identity without holding the
departed connection. If another write owns the retention shard, the Will
waits in the shard's FIFO under the existing pending-byte budget. Commit
updates the retained index before live routing. The broker holds detached
work until the APP completion retires, including during shutdown.

The independent peer checked a Will contending with an active retained
write, orderly delivery, restart recovery, delayed cancellation on
reconnect, session expiry before Will Delay, and an MQTT 3.1.1 Will
tombstone. TLS, WS and WSS checks observed actual retained Will delivery
after Disconnect with Will Message. The unit fixture restored a due Will,
held its APP completion after the expiry timer retired, and verified the
broker stayed unjoined until the detached write completed.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed modular and single-header probes,
TCP regressions and static and shared package consumers. WSL ASan/UBSan
with leak checking and TSan passed the unit and independent tests. Raw
evidence is under
out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-retained-will-*.

Armed Wills remain covered by controlled session checkpoints. Live
persistence of armed Wills, recipient queues and inbound QoS 2 deduplication,
native Linux, controlled performance comparisons and 72-hour mixed loads
remain open.


## 2026-11-20 MQTT durable session reset before CONNACK

The optional broker store can commit removal of a Client ID's old session
records before success CONNACK for a fresh session. The broker waits for the
application completion on the connection's worker and preserves buffered
input order. One reset can be in flight per Client ID. Resumes bypass the
callback. A definite rejection refuses the connection and an unknown result
seals admission and invalidates session checkpoint export. The checkpoint
APP sample removes that client's record group, including any incoming QoS 2
identifiers, by atomic file replacement on a bounded writer pool.

Independent TCP tests killed the broker before and after the commit, verified
same-ID exclusion, checked the success CONNACK and coalesced PING order, and
confirmed that the unrelated session and its QoS 2 record survived. The same
tests forced a storage read rejection and a rejected atomic replacement,
then checked retirement of an in-flight completion during shutdown.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed modular and single-header restart
probes and static and shared package consumers. The retained-commit
regression passed TCP, TLS, WS and WSS. WSL ASan/UBSan with leak checking
and TSan passed the store tests and restart probes. Raw evidence is under
`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-session-reset-*`.

The test file backend was checked against process termination. Live QoS 2
deduplication and recipient queues still need an online commit path. The
strict release check reports 43 developing modules. Native Linux performance
comparisons and the Windows/Linux 72-hour mixed-load gates remain open.


## 2026-11-20 MQTT durable retirement of restored inbound QoS 2 IDs

The broker can now commit removal of an incoming QoS 2 identifier restored
from a checkpoint before sending PUBCOMP. This closes the stale-identifier
window when another process starts from the same checkpoint after the sender
has completed its exchange. The session commit callback also accepts the
existing fresh-session discard operation. The compatibility reset API is
still available. IDs accepted only in memory finish without a storage call.

The checkpoint APP example atomically removes one record or the whole Client
ID group on its storage worker. Definitive removal failure closes the
affected connection and preserves the pending exchange for resume. Unknown
outcomes close broker admission and invalidate export. A committed removal
also retires the ID when the original connection is gone.

Independent MQTT 5.0 and 3.1.1 peers verified identifier reuse across
restarts and ordered PUBCOMP with a coalesced PING. Probes covered process
termination before commit, known storage rejection and retry, takeover while
a commit was pending with no PUBCOMP on the old connection, an unknown
outcome, and preservation of unrelated IDs. Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64
passed modular, single-header, static and shared package verification, the
default TCP broker and retained TCP/TLS/WS/WSS regression. WSL ASan/UBSan
with leak checking and TSan passed the store suite and restart probes. Raw
evidence is under
`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-pubrel-*`.

Online acceptance of new inbound QoS 2 PUBLISH packets still needs an atomic
commit with the corresponding recipient delivery obligations. Native Linux,
performance comparisons and 72-hour workloads remain open. Strict release
still reports 43 developing modules.


## 2026-11-20 MQTT QoS 2 recipient admission before PUBREC

A new non-retained QoS 2 publish reserves all eligible reliable recipient
deliveries before the broker forwards to any subscriber. Reservations reuse
the existing per-session count, broker count and broker byte limits. The
recipient batch shares encoded frames. Allocation failure or insufficient
queue capacity rolls the batch back and returns MQTT 5 PUBREC 0x97. MQTT
3.1.1 closes the publishing connection on that failure. Existing subscriber
queues survive. Queue admission and dispatch are separate, and prepared
deliveries pin their selected session across dispatch after routing locks
are released. A retired session discards its reservation.

The socket fixture saturated an offline session and verified that the
hard refusal produced neither reliable live delivery nor best-effort
shared delivery. It then freed capacity and reused the same identifier,
verifying successful ordinary, offline and shared delivery. The
single-header fixture injected OOM after the first reservation, checked
charge rollback and retried with a recipient retired before dispatch.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed modular and single-header suites,
static and shared consumers, independent MQTT 5.0 and 3.1.1 TCP tests,
checkpoint restart and retained commit regressions across TCP, TLS, WS and
WSS. WSL ASan/UBSan with leak checking and TSan passed. Raw evidence is under
`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-qos2-fanout-*`.

A local QoS 2 loopback comparison against `64e0cab1` used the same GCC
`-O2` workload and XRT objects on each host, two workers, six interleaved
samples and one warm-up per revision. With 64 subscribers, the Windows
median was 85,170 to 89,414 deliveries/s and P99 was 1,026 to 987 us.
On WSL it was 46,602 to 46,822 deliveries/s and 1,552 to 1,546 us.
The one-subscriber throughput medians moved by less than 1% on each host.
The single-subscriber WSL tail samples had high variance. Requested
allocations per delivery were effectively unchanged in all cases. The
unbound local comparison covers this workload only.

The recipient batch is an in-memory admission stage. Durably accepting a
new QoS 2 publish still needs a single APP transaction covering the inbound
identifier and durable recipient obligations. Retained-route composition,
native Linux acceptance and the 72-hour gates remain open. Strict release
still reports 43 developing modules.


## 2026-11-20 MQTT atomic non-retained QoS 2 acceptance

The optional session transaction API submits the inbound QoS 2 identifier
and the queued records for persistent recipients in one APP transaction.
The broker waits for completion before sending a successful PUBREC or
dispatching the prepared deliveries. Reliable reservations take precedence
over temporary QoS 0 delivery reserves. Determinate refusal releases the
batch and an unknown outcome seals admission. PUBREL removes the durable
source identifier through the same keyed backend before PUBCOMP.

Persistent session keys survive normal resume and checkpoint recovery. A
fresh session gets a different key even when its Client ID is reused.
Recipient records include the Client ID and key so the backend can avoid
writing to a replacement session. The v3 file example implements the
transaction with an atomic image replacement and a bounded APP writer.
Its controlled restore path can still read v1/v2 files.

Independent TCP peers verified process termination before and after commit,
delayed best-effort dispatch, restored duplicate suppression, delivery to
two recovered offline sessions of both MQTT versions, finite message
expiry metadata, explicit rejection, unknown outcome, and a replacement
session which received none of its predecessor's queued data. A volatile
publisher with durable recipients exercised the transaction without a
source record. The final checkpoint run also covered an unkeyed v2 session
image and rejection of an invalid v3 SENT lifetime. An earlier executable
built before the timed-record fix accepted that malformed SENT fixture.
The rebuilt example and single-header binaries reject it.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed modular and single-header tests,
static and shared package consumers and the separate TCP and retained
transport regressions. WSL ASan/UBSan with leak checking and TSan passed
the store suites and transaction restart tests. Raw evidence is under
`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-qos2-transaction-*`.

Retained QoS 2 acceptance still needs composition with this transaction.
The outgoing SENT and terminal acknowledgement phases, as well as live
updates to subscriptions and session expiry, still use controlled
checkpoints. Native Linux performance and 72-hour mixed loads remain
open. Strict release reports 43 developing modules.


## 2026-11-20 MQTT retained QoS 2 joined to the acceptance transaction

Applications can explicitly enable retained QoS 2 composition once both
commit hooks point at their authoritative store. The session transaction
then applies the retained replacement or deletion, the inbound identifier
and durable recipient queues together before PUBREC. Prepared delivery and
retention state become visible after confirmation. The retained-only path
still handles QoS 0, QoS 1 and triggered Wills. The two paths share the
existing shard reservations and retention budgets.

The v4 file example uses one bounded writer for both hooks. It records a
capture offset per retained value and preserves prior file read support.
The independent TCP probes covered process termination around the combined
commit, duplicate replay, offline recovery, competing same-shard writes,
explicit refusal, unknown outcome, empty retained PUBLISH and expiry while
the commit was pending. Both MQTT 5.0 and 3.1.1 were exercised.

The pre-fix writer-saturation probe reproduced an input-order failure when
the APP refused a ticket inline. The broker now pauses and drains input only
for an accepted deferred commit. Inline refusal keeps the native read
callback in control. The probe repeats PUBREC 0x83 and PINGRESP on the same
connection and verifies that the retained reservation is released.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed modular, single-header, static and
shared tests. The retained-only transport regressions passed TCP, TLS, WS
and WSS. WSL ASan/UBSan with leak checking and TSan passed the retained
limit tests and combined checkpoint probes. Raw evidence is under
`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-qos2-retained-transaction-*`.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT online outbound acknowledgement phases

The optional outbound transactions use a stable delivery key to distinguish
reliable recipients, including two queued messages with identical bytes.
The broker commits the original Packet Identifier and first ACK phase
before PUBLISH, then commits the PUBCOMP phase before PUBREL. The
terminal ACK or a broker discard retires the record. Definitive refusal
leaves the previous phase available for resume and closes the affected
connection. Unknown outcomes close admission.

The APP-owned v5 checkpoint keeps delivery keys and preserves actual
first-send order when multiple publishers write concurrently. It uses the
existing bounded writer and atomic image replacement. It reads v3 through v5
in online mode and v1 through v5 in controlled mode. The independent TCP
probes covered termination with an uncommitted first send, original
identifiers and DUP on resumed PUBLISH, PUBREL on restart and takeover,
terminal PUBCOMP and negative PUBREC, PUBACK for MQTT 5.0 and 3.1.1,
a reduced Maximum Packet Size at reconnect, v4 upgrade, backend rejection
and an unknown backend outcome.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed the broker and store suites,
modular and single-header checkpoint probes, and static and shared
package consumers. Independent TCP handshake and retained-commit transport
probes passed, including TLS, WS and WSS for retained commits. WSL ASan/UBSan
with leak checking and TSan passed broker and store suites plus the final
modular checkpoint probe. Raw evidence is under
`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-outbound/`.

Online outbound progress applies to records created by the online acceptance
hook. Controlled checkpoints still cover zero-key deliveries and updates
to subscriptions and session expiry. Native Linux performance and the
72-hour acceptance workloads are open. Strict release reports 43
developing modules.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT online QoS 1 recipient persistence

The optional QoS 1 transaction reuses bounded recipient reservation and
the keyed outbound lifecycle. The APP commits reliable durable recipient
queues before the broker releases delivery and sends a success PUBACK.
When combined retained transactions are enabled, the retained replacement
or deletion shares the same commit. No inbound identifier is stored for
QoS 1, so a retry can deliver a duplicate. A definite refusal sends a
negative MQTT 5 PUBACK or closes MQTT 3.1.1 before acknowledging. Unknown
effects seal admission. The default memory-only path keeps its original
admission behavior.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT online subscription transactions

A persistent session can opt in to committing one set of acknowledged
subscription edits per request. New links reserve topic, group and global
capacity outside the routing lists. Existing link options and membership
stay active during the write. Confirmation publishes additions and
removals before SUBACK or UNSUBACK. Definite failure rolls back new
reservations and preserves prior routing. MQTT 5 emits per-filter
failure reasons, and MQTT 3.1.1 closes on a failed unsubscribe.

The APP checkpoint writer applies the final edit for each filter and
share pair against the keyed session. It preserves distinct groups, all

## 2026-11-20 MQTT online session expiry

The optional session lifecycle operations persist the negotiated interval
before a fresh or resumed persistent CONNECT succeeds. They reserve the
close ticket up front and record the network-close time after earlier
protocol work drains. MQTT 5 DISCONNECT overrides apply to that close,
and a zero lifetime removes the record. A reconnect admitted before
expiry keeps its reservation across store delay. A later CONNECT gets a
fresh session. A failed close commit seals the broker.

The APP example adds an online expiry mode and a version 6 checkpoint
marker for connected sessions. Observed closures retain their offline
deadlines. After a process kill with no observed close, the example
rebases the interval at the first recovery and writes the result before
opening the listener. It accounts for writer delay and reads the older
supported formats.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL passed modular and single-header broker
storage and checkpoint TCP coverage, static and shared package consumers,
and four session-resume and takeover benchmark smoke cases per platform.
The independent process probe checked long live sessions, recovery through
two starts, shortening and deleting on disconnect, resume interval changes,
takeover, reconnects around expiry during a delayed write, MQTT 3.1.1,
in-process Will timing and close-store rejection. WSL ASan/UBSan,
leak detection and TSan also passed the complete TCP checkpoint probe.

Raw evidence is under
`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-session-expiry/`.
Strict release still reports 43 developing modules. Durable armed and
delayed Wills, controlled performance comparisons, native Linux and
72-hour production acceptance remain open.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT durable publication of saved Wills

The optional Will transaction carries the keyed retirement of a restored
delayed Will, any retained mutation, and the durable recipient queues.
The broker releases prepared routing only after the write commits. A
resume admitted before the delay cancels the saved record in the same
write as the new session state. A due Will pins its source until the
transaction retires. Clean Start can bring the prior Will due and can
return Server Busy while the pending state drains.

The TCP checkpoint probes cover a killed process during a pending write,
definite store rejection, a second restart after commit, one queued
QoS 1 delivery to an offline QoS 2 subscriber, retained replacement,
resume cancellation across the deadline, and Clean Start retirement.
The default in-memory Will profile passed two smoke workloads on each
platform. Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL passed modular, single-header,
static and shared checks, and WSL passed ASan/UBSan, leak detection and
TSan on the checkpoint probe.

Raw evidence is under
`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-stored-will/`.
The ordinary maturity check passes. Strict release still reports 43
developing modules. Arming new Wills in online storage and persisting the
delay on native disconnect remain open. Native Linux performance and
72-hour production acceptance are also open.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT online Will transactions

With online Will storage enabled, START and RESUME commit the canonical
Will and its delay before CONNACK. Normal DISCONNECT commits cancellation
and the negotiated expiry interval before finishing the transport. CLOSE
schedules the Will from the observed network-close time, bounded by
session expiry. Zero-expiry connections reserve a keyed session until
cancellation or publication. Clean Start and immediate Wills can fence
takeover until the previous Will retires.

The APP example version 7 records a per-Will time. It starts the delay at
the first recovery when no close was observed and writes the result before
opening its listener. A later restart uses the recorded deadline.
Publication continues to retire the keyed Will in the same write as
retained state and durable recipient deliveries.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL passed broker storage tests, the full
checkpoint TCP probe with modular and single-header builds, and static
and shared package consumers. The new probe checks two successive process
terminations, cancellation, DISCONNECT expiry override, same-ID resume and
Clean Start, and zero-expiry Will recovery in MQTT 5 and MQTT 3.1.1.
A dedicated MQTT 3.1.1 case kills the broker after cancellation commits
and before CLOSE commits. It reproduced startup rejection before the fix
and now verifies a fresh session with the Will still cancelled.
The complete WSL checkpoint probe passed ASan/UBSan with leak detection
and TSan. The default in-memory Will workload passed both smoke cases
on each platform.

`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-online-will/`.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT APP processing of durable pending publications

Removed the library's durable Inbox leases, lease cookies and application
dispatch state. Applications create the semantic Writer, copy the oldest
committed pending record and decide when to process and retire it. They can
assign disjoint keys for parallel processing. The Writer retires the exact
record by its stored epoch and key in the existing commit FIFO. Pending
records have a committed index with constant-time head selection and
unlinking. The index carries no consumer ownership.

Retirement uses the existing INBOX_ACK journal format. It rejects stale
epochs and retired keys before I/O and leaves MQTT QoS 2 receive
identity and protocol acknowledgement ordering intact. The APP checks
the commit effect before advancing and reconciles after uncertain results.
Both the simple real-file example and the reconnect example apply this
contract. The initial test run exposed an omitted copy of staged
record metadata. The copy is restored, keeping the pending index in the
committed model only.

The pending record suite exercises short and overlapping outputs, OOM,
out-of-order APP retirement, stale epochs and duplicates, late commit,
storage failures, uncertain recovery and native partitioned consumers.
It passes WSL ASan/UBSan with leak detection and TSan. Windows x64 and
Ubuntu/WSL passed eleven modular and single-header suites covering the
journal, writer, durable TCP/TLS/auth/WS clients, reconnect and
compaction. Both environments passed static/shared consumers, four
capacity smoke cases and the real-file APP example.

Windows and WSL clients passed 24 Mosquitto 2.1.2 cases in total over
TCP and WSS through an independent TLS 1.3 gateway. They exercise
MQTT 5 and 3.1.1 with withheld PUBACK, PUBREC and PUBCOMP, then
verify the APP retirement after reopening the journal.

Raw evidence is under
`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-app-durable-records/`.
Ordinary maturity passes. Strict release still reports 41 developing
MQTT modules. The concrete storage backends, native Linux qualification,
controlled performance comparisons and 72-hour mixed loads remain open.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT offline checkpoints and APP compaction

The APP example closes the selected Journal, prepares the inactive
generation, writes the checkpoint and publishes the selector. The

A recovered checkpoint owns the validated raw protocol state, including
the original expiry fields, and can be written to an empty matching
Journal supplied by the APP. The checkpoint module depends on typed
recovery. File provisioning, the selector and maintenance timing
belong to the caller.

selector publication separately. The initial compiler pass exposed a

The APP callback decides the minimum reclaim, measures the framed

## 2026-11-20 MQTT QoS 1 and QoS 2 fixed-arrival broker comparison

The observer now completes both sides of the MQTT 5 reliable exchange.
It recycles publisher packet identifiers only after PUBACK or PUBCOMP
and tracks the broker's subscriber identifiers independently. Each
reliable repeat uses the requested window in the observer and advertises
it to the broker on subscriber connections. The publisher verifies the
broker's Receive Maximum. The queue settings give each subscriber 256
pending slots, including the active window.

Publisher P99 ends at the received terminal acknowledgement. Subscriber
P99 ends when its terminal acknowledgement has been sent. Both begin at
the scheduled publication time, including waiting for a publisher credit.
The observer checks publisher and subscriber counts and drains both sides.
A scripted peer reproduces early PUBCOMP, wrong PUBCOMP identity and
duplicate subscriber delivery. The first Windows failure probe left a
blocking reader waiting. The observer now bounds individual socket
operations and all three regressions pass on both environments.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL each completed 112 reliable repeats against
Mosquitto 2.1.2 with the same observer and CPU budget. Each sample checked
3,000 publisher confirmations and the full subscriber delivery set after
300 warmups. The exact-filter scenario used one subscriber and 2,000
publications/s. The wildcard scenario used eight subscribers and 3,000
publications/s. The table gives medians of seven repeats in the latter
scenario. Each result column shows xmqtt / Mosquitto.

| Environment | QoS | Window | Deliveries/s | Publisher P99 (us) | Subscriber P99 (us) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |

| Windows x64 | 1 | 16 | 24,003 / 24,003 | 53.8 / 594.2 | 219.8 / 923.9 |
| Windows x64 | 2 | 1 | 23,986 / 24,000 | 16,532.5 / 6,684.5 | 16,776.1 / 6,768.5 |

| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | 1 | 1 | 24,002 / 24,000 | 111.2 / 726.8 | 466.6 / 1,283.4 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | 1 | 16 | 24,001 / 23,998 | 91.4 / 523.3 | 341.5 / 416.7 |

The variation gates passed 31 of 32 ingress series and one of 64 P99

## 2026-11-20 Redis fixed-arrival Hiredis reference

The existing ECHO benchmark now builds a Hiredis 1.3.0 reference beside
the xredis observer. They share a fixed RESP3 arrival schedule, binary
reply checks, a bounded outstanding window, and timing from scheduled
arrival to reply observation. The xredis observer drives one XRT worker
plus the generator. Hiredis drives its socket and parser from the generator.
The paired runner alternates order and retains every sample, including
samples with rejected offers.

Native Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 clients each used a two-logical-CPU
budget and a dedicated, single-CPU Redis 8.0.5 process in WSL. Windows
connected through WSL loopback forwarding. Persistence was disabled.
Each case ran seven three-second samples per client plus one warmup.
Across 140 measured samples, 2,133,826 of 2,142,000 offers were admitted.
The Redis command counter matched the admitted-offer ledger in all ten
cases. Every admitted binary reply validated before its deadline.

| Offers/s | Payload (bytes) | Window | Windows rejected (xredis / Hiredis) | WSL rejected (xredis / Hiredis) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 500 | 32 | 1 | 38 / 10 | 7 / 6 |
| 2,000 | 32 | 128 | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| 3,000 | 1,024 | 16 | 146 / 14 | 0 / 0 |
| 5,000 | 32 | 16 | 410 / 307 | 0 / 0 |
| 15,000 | 32 | 64 | 5,354 / 1,715 | 0 / 167 |

All rejections in the table occurred when the observer's outstanding
window was full. Neither client reported server errors or timeouts.
The WSL pairs at 3,000 and 5,000 offers/s fully delivered the offered load.
Their P99 medians were 150.5 / 81.3 us and 141.2 / 71.3 us respectively.
Only the 5,000/s xredis P99 series passed the existing 3% MAD and 6%
central-range limits among those four P99 series. The 2,000/s control
completed every offer on both platforms. Its P99 medians were
272.9 / 227.2 us on Windows and 180.8 / 84.0 us on WSL. All four
control P99 series failed at least one variation limit.

Both platforms passed the modular and single-header open-loop regressions.

and a held reply in excess of its deadline each fail the run. Ordinary

Two separately supervised native processes exercise the public xmqtt

connection verifies the retained replay. A tombstone removes the record

The TCP APP accepts an explicit connection count. Each connection has

share one bounded XRT executor. The APP retires socket writes per peer
and drains the executor before releasing job and event storage. The
APP owns transport and executor policy. The independent peer
verified 512 parallel replies per mode and confirmed that another
connection still completed its 128 replies after an oversized record
closed the offending connection.

The fixed-arrival comparison uses eight requests per batch and 1,600

identity and order, including for separate clients. Both modes use the
same workers, framing and CPU allowance. The reader measures latency
from the scheduled arrival and reports offer lag separately. Windows
x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 ran five repeats each with one connection and one
worker, four connections and two workers, and eight connections with
either one or two workers.

## 2026-11-20 Redis recovery across a real process restart

One xredis process kept its shared pool and subscription session through
forced termination and replacement of an owned Redis 8.0.5 fixture. A
separate observer identified the fixture and confirmed BLPOP had blocked.
The original Future reported DISCONNECTED and MAY_HAVE_EXECUTED without
a reply and retained that outcome after recovery. The pool retired both
established members and rejected a call during the outage without
overwriting the caller's Future. Both the pool and subscription session
observed failed reconnects before the observer started the replacement.

The replacement used a different Redis process ID and run ID on the same
port. Two pool members became ready and the subscription session restored
the existing binary channel intent in generation two. The APP opened a
fresh Tracking connection and verified receive order and key identity on
invalidation. The client also verified one binary publication and all 16
post-recovery pipelined replies. Independent server command counts matched the
expected ledger at each phase. No BLPOP or rejected PING reached the replacement.
After teardown, Redis reported only the observer connection.

| Client configuration | Completed restarts | Recovery min / median / max in ms |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Windows x64, GCC 16.2 | 7 / 7 | 139.270 / 184.714 / 1229.657 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64, GCC 15.2 | 7 / 7 | 95.940 / 127.004 / 143.365 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64, ASan/UBSan with leak detection | 7 / 7 | 119.569 / 136.258 / 165.111 |

The Redis fixture ran in Ubuntu/WSL for every case. Timings start after
observation of the old dedicated connections' physical closes and include
the failed reconnect barrier, fixture replacement and verification of
resumed traffic. The Windows path included WSL loopback forwarding. These
observations cover standalone RESP3 over plaintext TCP. Native Linux and
72-hour acceptance remain open. The ordinary maturity check passed and
the strict xredis gate failed with 29 developing modules.

The initial fixture invocation followed a multi-call Redis symlink and
ran the wrong entry point. An early probe sampled generation retirement
before the worker had finished it, and one repetition reused a port that
was still unavailable. The final series keeps the Redis invocation name,
waits for physical retirement and failed replacement attempts, and uses
a fresh screened port every time. The failed attempts, per-case results
and qualification summary are under
out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xredis-restart-recovery/.
See [the xredis reproduction guide](../../extlibs/xredis/docs/client-performance.md#recovery-across-a-redis-process-restart).

## 2026-11-20 MQTT QoS 2 independent publisher and subscriber windows

The fixed-arrival observer now controls publisher credits and subscriber
Receive Maximum separately. Each accepted repeat reports the scheduled
arrival-to-pacer lag, current publisher slot wait, number of arrivals
that found a busy slot, and PUBLISH send-to-terminal-ack latency. The
original end-to-end percentiles still include all queueing. The observer
retains the reason code when it sees a negative acknowledgement or a
DISCONNECT. In particular, PUBREC 0x97 terminates the repeat as a quota
rejection. Only successful terminal acknowledgements count as confirmations.

The Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL matrices each used one xmqtt broker worker
or Mosquitto 2.1.2, one broker logical CPU, three disjoint observer
logical CPUs, one publisher, eight wildcard subscribers, plaintext TCP,
and in-memory state. Each window pair ran seven repetitions per broker,
with 300 warmups and 3,000 measured publications at 3,000/s. The
110 complete repetitions verified 330,000 terminal publisher responses
and 2,640,000 payload-checked deliveries. Table values are medians of
completed repeats. The WSL 16/1 xmqtt row covers five of seven attempts.

| Environment | Publisher / subscriber window | xmqtt publisher credit stalls out of 3,000 | xmqtt P99 from send in ms | xmqtt / Mosquitto delivery P99 in ms |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Windows x64 | 1 / 1 | 1,826 | 0.506 | 12.601 / 11.371 |
| Windows x64 | 1 / 16 | 1,402 | 0.501 | 10.271 / 11.713 |
| Windows x64 | 16 / 1 | 5 | 3.246 | 15.250 / 9.523 |
| Windows x64 | 16 / 16 | 29 | 8.952 | 9.547 / 10.022 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | 1 / 1 | 3,000 | 0.494 | 9.848 / 3.816 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | 1 / 16 | 2,907 | 0.590 | 85.735 / 3.636 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | 16 / 1 | 0 | 0.589 | 52.415 / 2.367 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | 16 / 16 | 0 | 0.903 | 1.265 / 2.991 |

In WSL, the 1/16 publisher reached scheduled arrivals with 85.034 ms
P99 lag while the send-to-confirmation P99 was 0.590 ms. Most arrivals
waited for a publisher slot and the backlog accumulated across rounds.
With 16/1, completed repeats saw no publisher credit stalls and a
52.415 ms subscriber delivery P99. Two repeats ended with PUBREC 0x97.
The 16/16 profile sustained 2,999.27 publications/s and 23,994.17
deliveries/s on WSL. This isolates a narrow subscriber window as a second

credit. Windows completed all window combinations and still showed

Of the 14 throughput series from fully completed pairs, 13 met the
existing noise gate. None of their 28 publisher or delivery P99 series
met it. The release performance baseline, native Linux qualification,

## 2026-11-20 MQTT QoS 2 fan-out under uneven subscriber pressure

The broker regression uses one worker, ten wildcard subscribers, Receive
Maximum one and a two-delivery cap per destination. It fills each
recipient's two credits, finishes both exchanges on nine subscribers and
leaves the tenth full. The next PUBLISH receives PUBREC 0x97. The nine
available subscribers answer PING without an unexpected delivery. The
broker retains the two outstanding obligations at the slow subscriber.
After it drains, the publisher reuses the rejected packet ID and all ten
subscribers receive the new payload in order. Final accounting verifies
30 forwards, one rejected publication, zero dropped deliveries and zero
remaining reliable deliveries and bytes.

A production experiment grouped contiguous ready nonpersistent deliveries
on the current worker in one native post per group of up to eight. It used
two worker callbacks for a ten-recipient publication. The source, generated
header and test diff are retained with the experiment.

The comparison paired the baseline at 5294e5f6 with the experiment built by
the same compiler. Both used the same external observer, one broker worker,
one broker logical CPU and three disjoint observer logical CPUs, one
publisher, eight wildcard subscribers, in-memory MQTT 5 and plaintext TCP.
Each pair alternated order and ran seven times on Windows and WSL. A complete
run verified 3,000 publisher confirmations and 24,000 deliveries after 300
warmups. Across 112 attempts, 98 completed and verified 294,000 confirmations
and 2,352,000 deliveries. All 14 incomplete attempts reported PUBREC 0x97.

| Environment | Publisher / subscriber window | Target publications/s | Complete runs, baseline / experiment | Delivery P99 median in ms, baseline / experiment |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Windows x64 | 16 / 1 | 3,000 | 7 / 6 | 30.655 / 10.394 |
| Windows x64 | 16 / 16 | 3,000 | 7 / 7 | 5.195 / 8.505 |
| Windows x64 | 1 / 16 | 3,000 | 7 / 7 | 3.858 / 3.500 |
| Windows x64 | 16 / 1 | 2,000 | 7 / 7 | 5.882 / 6.094 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | 16 / 1 | 3,000 | 0 / 1 | unavailable / 78.182 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | 16 / 16 | 3,000 | 7 / 7 | 3.765 / 4.257 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | 1 / 16 | 3,000 | 7 / 7 | 237.688 / 222.804 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | 16 / 1 | 2,000 | 7 / 7 | 3.635 / 8.204 |

All 12 delivery P99 series from complete A/B pairs exceeded the existing
variation limits. Throughput was close for profiles that both builds completed. The
experiment reduced native posts and produced mixed tail results with no
qualified net improvement. The commit ships the uneven-pressure recovery
case and leaves the experiment in the evidence directory. The narrowed
subscriber window at the higher rate remains an unresolved performance
and overload condition.

The experiment passed the Windows and WSL modular and single-header broker
suites, MQTT 3.1.1/5 and checkpoint tests, and 30-second mixed-load smokes.
The WSL single-header suite passed ASan/UBSan with leak detection. The
uneven-pressure regression was then built on the original runtime and
passed Windows and WSL modular and single-header suites and WSL ASan/UBSan
with leak detection. The asset checks passed and strict release still
reports 39 developing modules.

The A/B runner, per-repeat ledgers, failed rounds, candidate patch and
verification logs are under
out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-local-fanout/.

## 2026-11-20 xrpc bounded-window TCP saturation sweep

The TCP observer now uses a separate sender and reply reader per
connection. A batch occupies one observer slot until its final matching
reply. Scheduled arrivals remain in the latency denominator when the
window fills. Each run verifies every reply in order within five
seconds and reconciles the APP's full executor ledger. Latency starts
at the scheduled arrival. Offer lag, window wait and send-to-reply
percentiles are reported separately.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 each ran five repetitions per mode
with eight connections, sixteen batches in flight per connection,
and 4,800 measured calls plus 64 warmups per connection. The APP
was pinned to logical CPUs 2,4 and the observer to 6,8,10. The
two-worker sweep used six offered rates from 12,800 to 256,000
calls/s in aggregate. The one-worker sweep used 64,000 and 128,000
calls/s. The duplex and dispatch-only APP modes shared framing,
the executor and CPU placement. All 160 samples matched the APP
and observer ledgers, for 6,144,000 verified measured replies.

| Environment | Workers | Offered calls/s | Verified replies/s, duplex / dispatch | P99 in ms, duplex / dispatch |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Windows | 2 | 64,000 | 62,947 / 62,629 | 1.721 / 1.447 |
| Windows | 1 | 128,000 | 121,081 / 124,087 | 12.909 / 4.333 |
| Windows | 2 | 128,000 | 122,143 / 123,539 | 3.195 / 4.972 |
| Windows | 2 | 256,000 | 145,644 / 184,538 | 121.210 / 78.953 |
| Ubuntu/WSL | 2 | 64,000 | 63,044 / 63,296 | 2.161 / 1.940 |
| Ubuntu/WSL | 1 | 128,000 | 71,450 / 86,897 | 233.848 / 144.960 |
| Ubuntu/WSL | 2 | 128,000 | 122,128 / 123,373 | 15.544 / 9.762 |
| Ubuntu/WSL | 2 | 256,000 | 89,230 / 93,655 | 270.007 / 252.537 |

At the last two offered rates, the duplex windows reached their full
sixteen batches in both environments. At 256,000 offered calls/s,
duplex offer-lag P99 was 119.358 ms on Windows and 260.577 ms on WSL.
The corresponding P99 after the send attempt was 16.783 ms and
14.970 ms. The arrival-to-reply tails include the waiting time. The
top rate offers its 4,800 calls per connection in about 0.15 seconds,
then drains. The data describes the offered bursts on this host.

Of 32 comparable series, 27 throughput and 9 tail-latency series met
the existing variation limits. Native Linux, a stable release tail
baseline and the strict release gate remain open. Ordinary maturity
and generated asset checks passed. Strict release reports xrpc and
xrpc_duplex as developing.

Windows and WSL passed TCP interoperability, the original closed-loop
and concurrent modes, and the one-batch-window smoke. The socket-pair
checks verified the one-batch limit and rejected a mismatched ID and
an extra reply. WSL ASan/UBSan with leak detection passed a 1,003-call
sweep whose last batch was partial. The first standalone build omitted
the XRT event feature; the successful binaries enabled it explicitly.

## 2026-11-20 xcron scheduler clock steps and deadline bounds

The registered scheduler single-header test substitutes scripted wall and
monotonic observations and relative waits at the scheduler call sites.
The explicit Wake cases set and consume the native XRT event. The host
clock and the native core remain available to the existing test suite.

The forward-step case wakes the owner, delivers every late job once in
registration order and preserves the advanced deadline on rollback. The
backward-step case observes a 250 ms initial wait and exactly 750 ms
remaining in the original 1,000 ms monotonic budget. A callback advancing
the scripted wall clock leaves the current dispatch wave's cutoff intact.
Clock-loss cases preserve caller output and pending jobs through recovery.
The int64 endpoint case exercises wait-delay saturation, delivery of the
last representable occurrence and return of the job slot.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 passed the full modular and single-header
suites, including the new test, plus the restart catch-up subprocess test.
WSL ASan/UBSan with leak detection passed both scheduler suites and TSan
passed the native Wait and cross-thread Wake suite. Four deliberately
altered local test builds were rejected for replaying missed occurrences,
restarting a monotonic timeout, resampling inside a callback wave, and
wrapping a large wait delay.

Calendar and scheduler variants passed both static and shared consumer
checks. The initial concurrent packaging commands shared the x64 output
directory and the WSL link picked up Windows objects. The WSL verification
was repeated in the native package directory. The four Windows consumers
were re-run successfully after the isolated WSL build. The first failure
and the previous native package artifacts are retained in the evidence
directory.

Generated-header, feature and API checks and ordinary maturity pass.
Strict release still lists xcron and xcron_scheduler as developing.
Native Linux and release-grade performance evidence remain open.

out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xcron-clock-steps/.

## 2026-11-20 Redis mixed commands across one and four connections

The fixed-arrival observer runs the same RESP3 workload for xredis and
Hiredis 1.3.0. It assigns offers round-robin by connection, with one SET
followed by three GETs on each connection. The GET key is seeded once per
run before timing. Both clients check the binary GET value and the SET
status. HELLO and PING finish before timing on every connection. The
128-request observer window is shared across connections. xredis uses
one XRT I/O worker. The Hiredis generator services each connection's
nonblocking I/O and matches replies against its own FIFO.

The Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 observers used the same private
Redis 8.0.5 fixture design in WSL and 1,024-byte values. Each client ran
five two-second measured repetitions and one warmup per case. The client
affinity was CPUs 4 and 8. Redis was pinned to CPU 0. The Windows client
used WSL loopback forwarding. All 80 measured samples reconciled with
the server's GET, SET, HELLO and PING counts. The clients validated
1,119,337 replies out of 1,120,000 scheduled offers, including 839,508
GETs and 279,829 SETs. There were no malformed replies, missed deadlines
or client admission errors. xredis completed every scheduled offer.
