## 2026-11-20 xredis worker posts after ordinary replies

An ordinary reply now schedules another client turn when queued requests
can use the returned in-flight credit. Cancelling the timer of a retired
request releases its timer reference without a second wake request. New
submissions still post their own work. Cancel and timeout handling and the
reservation-drop wake for closing clients remain in force.

The A/B experiment used four RESP3 connections, 1,024-byte mixed GET/SET
data, a 128-request observer window, and five two-second samples per client
and case. Windows used loopback forwarding to the same design of private
WSL Redis 8.0.5 fixture as the WSL observer. Control and candidate completed
all 560,000 measured offers, with exact Redis command ledgers and identical
median timer-cancellation counts. The table shows per-sample medians.

| Observer | Offers/s | Executed worker posts, control / candidate | P99 in microseconds, control / candidate | Process CPU seconds, control / candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Windows | 2,000 | 12,046 / 8,042 | 819.3 / 734.3 | 2.141 / 2.094 |
| Windows | 12,000 | 71,194 / 47,634 | 960.6 / 843.8 | 2.516 / 2.625 |
| Ubuntu/WSL | 2,000 | 12,035 / 8,032 | 278.2 / 233.8 | 2.248 / 2.233 |
| Ubuntu/WSL | 12,000 | 71,861 / 47,983 | 220.3 / 227.9 | 3.089 / 3.028 |

The trace build measured admission, the worker handoff and send setup,
transport queue to final reader feed, the final feed and buffer consume,
and dispatch to just before promise resolution. At 12,000 offers/s in
WSL, the separate P99 medians were 3.0, 57.2, 133.7, 1.8 and 1.2
microseconds. These percentiles are computed separately. The transport
interval includes sending, Redis processing and receipt on the client
worker. The trace build completed 279,940 measured offers. Its Windows
high-load case had 60 observer-window rejections. The trace added request
storage and clock reads and ran only in the evidence binaries.

The in-flight regression holds a finite-timeout command against a
one-request wire window. A worker barrier proves the next command was
queued before release. Returning the reply completes the queued command
with its matching value and retires all physical obligations. The first
WSL modular sweep hit an intermittent TLS fixture stop failure. The
fixture now waits up to five seconds for the engine to retire after its
peer close notification. With identical runtime source from `100b57b0` and
an injected pin held for 500 ms after notification, the old fixture
rejected engine stop and the bounded wait passed. Delaying the callback
alone did not reproduce the stop failure. A separate mutation removed
the new reply-credit wake and failed the new queue regression.

The Windows suite passed, and the final client, TLS and open-loop single
headers passed focused Windows checks. The full WSL modular and single-header
suite passed on the rerun with the updated fixture. Static and shared
`xredis_client` packages passed independent consumers on Windows and WSL. The WSL client
suite passed ASan/UBSan with leak detection and a TSan run retaining GCC's
explicit warning for thread fences. A separate Windows `-O1` TLS build
hit warnings in the unchanged XRT single header. The `-O2` build passed.
Generated assets and ordinary maturity passed. Strict release remains
open with 29 developing modules.

out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xredis-client-wake/.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT 5 idle capacity and reconnect waves

The independent observer ran on logical CPU 4 while either xmqtt or

worker. Each broker's connection limit matched the requested cohort
of 1, 100, 1,000, 8,000 or 10,000 clean MQTT 5 connections. The

idle for two seconds, and checked PING replies before and after

and case. Of 100 samples, 94 completed. They verified 322,020 initial

## 2026-11-20 MQTT connection latency at descriptor table growth

The connection observer can record TCP dial and MQTT handshake durations
per successful connection. On WSL 6.18.33.2, moving either process to a
different logical CPU and reducing observer concurrency from 32 to 8
left a 27–36 ms median CONNECT P99 in the 1,000-client diagnostic.
The two segment times put most of the delay after TCP connected.

A socket trace matched clients to kernel resources by loopback source
port. It matched 9,999 of 10,000 connections in a five-pair diagnostic.
For the slowest 1% in each xmqtt run, the median interval between the
first completed CONNECT read and the CONNACK write was 12–13
microseconds. The long interval was before the broker read CONNECT.
A separate kernel trace mapped the worker's WSL PID via a trace
marker. In its complete retained window, `accept4` took 17.13, 11.49,
12.55 and 14.32 ms when returning descriptors 64, 128, 256 and 512.
The kernel expands the table at those boundaries and waits for an RCU
grace period when the process shares the table between threads.
Initial incomplete joins, PID mapping attempts and ring overruns are
preserved with the traces.
[WSL 6.18 descriptor table implementation](https://github.com/microsoft/WSL2-Linux-Kernel/blob/linux-msft-wsl-6.18.y/fs/file.c#L232-L260).

The Linux APP example now has an explicit `--prepare-fds` option.
It expands its descriptor table before starting the network worker.
At startup, the test observed 64 slots with the option disabled and
2,048 or 16,384 slots with it enabled for 1,000 or 10,000 requested
clients. The process held six open descriptors in each case. With a
soft limit of 64 and preparation requested above that limit, the
example exited before opening the listener.

The comparison used the same xmqtt binary with preparation off, then
on. The Mosquitto binary, CPU pins, 32-slot observer window, plaintext
MQTT and workload stayed fixed. All 40 samples completed, verifying
220,000 initial connections and 22,000 reconnects. Both brokers
returned their open-descriptor count to the baseline in every sample.

| 10,000 | 21.90 / 7.14 ms | 5.17 / 7.36 ms | 6,936 / 6,320 |

met the variation limit. The 1,000-client prepared P99 still varied

## 2026-11-20 xredis wakeups after TCP write drain

TCP drain and low-water notifications post a client turn when connection
initialization or transaction work can use it, pending requests have
in-flight credit, or the connection is closing. Ordinary submissions
post their own turns and replies return in-flight credit. This removes
the second client turn after an ordinary write drains with no pending
work.

The pressure test pauses a real loopback peer and bounds the socket
send buffer. One 256 KiB command occupies the transport queue and the
next waits for capacity while a worker barrier checks both states.
The peer withholds both replies until the second command arrives.
Resuming its reads makes the client advance using write credit, and
both results retain their FIFO identities. Removing the pending-write
wake from a separate WSL build caused this test to time out waiting
for a result.

The fixed-arrival comparison used four RESP3 connections, 1,024-byte
GET/SET values and a shared 128-request observer window. xredis control
and candidate used the same observer and XRT snapshot with an engine
counter read after retirement. A pinned Hiredis 1.3.0 binary from the
earlier mixed comparison served as the reference. Each platform used a
private WSL Redis 8.0.5 fixture pinned to CPU 0 and observers pinned to
CPUs 4 and 8. Windows accessed the fixture through loopback forwarding.
All 60 two-second measured samples and their warmups matched the Redis
command ledgers. All 840,000 measured offers completed.

| Observer | Offers/s | xredis worker posts, before / after | xredis process CPU seconds, before / after | P99 in microseconds, before / after / Hiredis |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Windows x64 | 2,000 | 8,042 / 4,037 | 2.094 / 2.078 | 351.9 / 335.5 / 294.9 |
| Windows x64 | 12,000 | 47,948 / 23,999 | 2.641 / 2.609 | 445.4 / 474.8 / 373.1 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | 2,000 | 8,042 / 4,037 | 2.226 / 2.213 | 217.6 / 215.2 / 119.8 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | 12,000 | 48,017 / 24,037 | 3.006 / 2.931 | 191.3 / 185.2 / 110.7 |

The table gives five-sample medians. Timer cancellation counts matched
between xredis variants in every case. The candidate's Windows and WSL
2,000-offer P99 series met the variation limits. Its two
12,000-offer P99 series exceeded the variation limits, and the Windows
median was higher than the control. Stable release P99 and native Linux
acceptance remain open.

The complete xredis test suite passed on Windows, including modular and
single-header builds. The focused single-header suite passed on WSL.
WSL ASan/UBSan
with leak detection and TSan passed, with GCC's thread-fence warning
retained in the TSan build. A Windows compiler diagnostic in the
existing invalid-configuration fixture was resolved by explicitly
initializing and checking its config. The initial Hiredis smoke used
the short client label and failed report validation. Repeating with

`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xredis-write-drain/`.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT receiver TCP acknowledgement timing

On Ubuntu/WSL x64, an isolated diagnostic build traced application delivery,
completion of the socket send call, and peer receipt for the last PUBACK of
each run. Both clients received 4,500 measured MQTT 5 QoS 1 messages at 3,000/s
with Receive Maximum 16 and the same 128-message warm-up. Each of the five
configurations passed seven measured repetitions and one process warm-up.

With Nagle enabled, the last PUBACK took more than 20 ms from the send return
to the peer in 7/7 xmqtt and 6/7 Paho repetitions. The 13 delays were
40.1–43.8 ms. In each one, `TCP_INFO` reported four bytes still unsent and one
unacknowledged segment after the call. The application had delivered the last
message at most 5.4 us before that send returned. Keeping xmqtt's default
`TCP_NODELAY` reduced its longest measured send-to-peer interval to 60.2 us.
Requesting immediate TCP ACKs on the peer while keeping Nagle enabled gave
maxima of 42.4 us for xmqtt and 45.4 us for Paho. These perturbations isolate
the final PUBACK delay to TCP buffering under this fixture's socket settings.

The receiver reference driver now exposes `--xmqtt-default-tcp` to retain
the TCP setting from `xmqttClientConfigInit`. The matched run enables Nagle
on both clients. The default-settings run uses `TCP_NODELAY` for xmqtt and
the default Paho socket setting.

Uninstrumented Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 runs verified 252,000 measured
deliveries and terminal acknowledgements across 56 samples, with eight
separate process warm-ups. The table shows the median of seven repetitions
per client and configuration for the same QoS 1 workload.

| Host | TCP settings | Verified/s, xmqtt / Paho | APP P99 in us, xmqtt / Paho | Terminal P99 in us, xmqtt / Paho |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Windows x64 | Matched | 3,000.6 / 3,000.6 | 247.7 / 291.7 | 352.1 / 391.9 |
| Windows x64 | Defaults | 3,000.6 / 3,000.6 | 211.0 / 199.6 | 293.6 / 284.1 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | Matched | 2,917.8 / 3,000.5 | 142.5 / 131.8 | 471.8 / 202.7 |
| Ubuntu/WSL x64 | Defaults | 3,000.5 / 2,917.4 | 137.4 / 138.6 | 210.5 / 453.2 |

## 2026-11-20 MQTT 5 receiver load through standalone Mosquitto

The receiver reference now supports a pinned Mosquitto 2.1.2 listener. A
raw publisher schedules 32-byte MQTT 5 publications at fixed times. The
subscriber relay validates the topic, payload, order and Receive Maximum
and tracks the two legs' packet IDs independently through PUBACK or
PUBREC/PUBREL/PUBCOMP. The application still validates every delivery.
PINGRESP on the broker's subscriber stream follows the forwarded final ACK
before a separate QoS 0 barrier releases the client for clean teardown.

The timed path buffers fragments per connection so a partial frame cannot
block the publisher waiting for the frame body. Measurements report offer
lag, application delivery, publisher-send-to-subscriber-ACK, and timed
relay-forward-to-subscriber-ACK separately. End-to-end times include the
relay's work. Mosquitto used a fourth logical CPU, `TCP_NODELAY` on its
sockets, plaintext TCP and no persistence. The two receiver executables
used matched TCP settings, with one live subscription per sample.

Native Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL x64 each completed the four-workload
matrix. The matrices verified 252,000 measured deliveries and acknowledgements
on both MQTT legs across 80 runs, with 16 process warm-ups. Each cell shows
the median of five runs per client. Terminal latency starts at the planned
offer and ends when the relay receives the subscriber's terminal ACK.

## 2026-11-20 xrpc TCP observer pacing and tail attribution

The phase probe matched one of every 31 APP documents to the independent
observer on both hosts. It recorded the scheduled offer, actual offer,
APP read and owner entry, executor submit/start/finish, owner resume,
APP send entry, and observer receipt. The 48 diagnostic samples verified
12,288,000 replies at 128,000 scheduled calls/s. The probe included the
uninstrumented build of the same APP in each comparison.

For duplex single-record traffic, the time before the observer's credit
check accounted for 92.9–96.7% of the cumulative latency of the slowest 1%
of the sampled replies on Windows, and 98.4–98.5% in Ubuntu/WSL. Each share
uses the same individual replies across all phases. Executor queue wait
and handler processing together contributed less than 0.1% in those runs.

The saturation observer now uses one event loop and a shared monotonic
schedule. All sockets use nonblocking I/O during the measured interval.
The observer resumes partial writes, verifies fragmented and coalesced
responses byte for byte, and keeps each connection's credit until the
entire group completes. It still measures every call against its
original schedule. A complete reply is timestamped at the socket read
that supplied its final bytes.

The A/B comparison used the same uninstrumented APP binary for both
observers on each host. Eight connections shared two workers with a
16-group window. Each run scheduled two seconds of traffic at 128,000
calls/s in total. APP CPUs were 0 and 2 and observer CPUs were 6, 8 and 10.
All 80 runs completed and verified 20,480,000 measured replies. Values

## 2026-11-20 xredis restart and TLS certificate rotation

The restart probe now supports verified TLS 1.3 with AES-128-GCM and

processes on one loopback port. The initial and final certificates
have different leaf identities signed by the same CA. The intermediate
certificate uses a separate CA. The independent observer verifies the
peer leaf, TLS profile, process identity and run ID on each listener.

The original process is killed after Redis observes the blocked BLPOP.

verification failure and observes additional failed pool and subscription

certificate. The probe verifies both recovered pool members, the binary
subscription intent, a fresh Tracking connection and ordered invalidation,
one binary publication and 16 pipelined replies. Redis observes the
expected command ledger and only the observer connection after client
teardown. The blocked Future retains its original outcome throughout.

## 2026-11-20 MQTT required broker authentication across restart

The ordinary CONNECT policy receives the decoded CONNECT fields without
the Authentication Method property. The optional auth module now offers
`xmqttServerCreateAuthRequired` for applications that require an enhanced
exchange on every connection. The broker refuses a method-less CONNECT
before policy callbacks, Will preparation or session claim. MQTT 5 returns
0x87 and MQTT 3.1.1 returns 0x05 when that version is enabled. Existing
`xmqttServerCreateAuth` callers retain the ordinary admission path and the
public configuration layout is unchanged.

The auth and checkpoint examples share their existing loopback proof
method. The APP selects required authentication again on restore. The
independent peer verifies two challenges and the final proof. Across
three broker processes it observes the pending binary QoS 1 delivery
after a successful CONNACK with Session Present. It checks DUP and
the original packet ID, then confirms
that the acknowledged delivery stays retired across the next restart.
The required policy denies method-less MQTT 5 and legacy connections
before the authenticated session resumes.

Windows and Ubuntu/WSL passed TCP, TLS, WS and WSS proof and admission
tests. Both passed the modular checkpoint sequence. The single-header
checkpoint sequence passed on Windows and under WSL ASan/UBSan with leak
detection. The standalone checkpoint build rejects the required option
when auth is absent. The full ordinary checkpoint peer passed in WSL.
On Windows that regression failed when its Will transaction observer
saw FileNotFoundError from stat during checkpoint replacement. Static
and shared consumers passed for the auth closure, and the Windows auth
limits and allocation rollback test passed. The controlled restart
regression is wired into the Windows and Linux interop jobs.

A separate Windows probe exercised the current `xrtFileWriteAtomic`
without a broker. Across three sets of 2,048 successful replacements,
an independent GetFileAttributesW observer recorded 23,629
ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND results in 832,928 checks after initial publication.
This reproduces the visibility gap while all writer calls report success.
The broader Windows checkpoint acceptance remains open.

Generated headers and API docs passed. Ordinary maturity checks passed.
Strict release still lists 39 developing xmqtt modules. Native Linux
runtime, authenticated crash-recovery load and release soak acceptance
remain open. The restart experiment uses controlled shutdown and the
local demonstration method. Evidence and binary/source hashes are under
`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-required-auth/`.
[Broker authentication and restart instructions](../../extlibs/xmqtt/docs/server.md#mqtt-5-enhanced-authentication).

The saturation observer can now stagger connections within each group
period. It retains the original arrival deadline even when a group has
to wait for credit, and records every connection phase in the report.
For the same slowest 1% of replies it sums offer delay outside observed
credit wait, observed credit wait and the interval from first send attempt
to receipt. Delay behind earlier unsent groups is part of the offer delay.

The comparison used the same APP binary and observer in both schedules.
Eight connections, two executor workers and 16 groups of outstanding
credit per connection scheduled 128,000 calls/s for two seconds. Aligned
offers had 64 calls due every 500 us. Staggered offers had eight calls due
every 62.5 us. APP CPUs were 0 and 2 and observer CPUs were 6, 8 and 10.

samples completed, verifying 20,480,000 replies. Each row is the median
of five runs per schedule.

## 2026-11-21 xcron integer and precise deadline comparison

An isolated build of the wait-phase fixture compared integer milliseconds
with a precise UTC occurrence mapped to a monotonic deadline. The precise
arm took a fractional wall sample and retained the caller's shorter
timeout. Windows used the same high-resolution waitable timer in both
arms. WSL ran a third arm with the precise scheduler deadline and the
original millisecond conversion inside the native condition wait.

Each host and job cohort used the same executable and pinned CPU 4 for
all its arms. Two processes per arm each measured 16 one-second waves.
The second repeat reversed arm order within each host and cohort.
The terminal journal and independently re-parsed raw output verified all
20 runs, 320 waves and 174,080 callbacks. No wave added a wait retry.

counter did not resolve these samples. The 32-wave series characterize

The experimental waiter passed expired-deadline event priority,

fallback retains its existing conversion. Poll and zero-time Wait still

## 2026-11-21 MQTT required authentication across process stops

The independent authentication peer now runs the online checkpoint
example over TCP. A publisher enqueues eight QoS 1 and nine QoS 2
messages for an offline subscriber and leaves one incoming QoS 2
exchange before PUBREL. The probe then stops its own broker process.
Every new broker uses the required authentication policy.

The resumed publisher retries the original QoS 2 PUBLISH and finishes
the exchange. The subscriber verifies that the resulting queue contains
each payload once. CONNECT without a method and CONNECT followed by an
invalid proof are rejected and leave the checkpoint bytes intact. A
paused authentication exchange remains silent, then the successful
CONNACK carries Session Present and the expected final proof before
the first replay packet.

The probe uses Receive Maximum one and checks the saved QoS 2 PUBREL
and the subsequent QoS 1 PUBLISH with DUP and its original packet ID
across separate process stops. The first trial showed that receiving a
new PUBLISH can precede committing an earlier PUBCOMP. The final
fixture waits for PINGRESP and verifies on-disk retirement before the
next cut. After acknowledging the last delivery, another process
recovers the session with an empty replay queue.

Windows and Ubuntu/WSL each passed ten repeated modular crash matrices.
They verified 80 deliberate process stops and 340 expected deliveries
in total. The full authentication probe on both hosts also passed
over TCP, TLS, WS and WSS, including the pre-existing controlled
checkpoint path. The crash case uses the TCP checkpoint example.
Both single-header versions passed the controlled and crash cases.
The WSL single-header run used ASan/UBSan with leak detection enabled.
The full ordinary checkpoint regression, generated header check and API
inventory also passed. Strict release still lists 39 developing modules.
Native Linux and 72-hour release acceptance remain open.

Source and binary hashes, process-stop reports and build logs are under
`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xmqtt-auth-crash-replay/`.
[Checkpoint authentication probe](../../extlibs/xmqtt/docs/server.md#mqtt-5-enhanced-authentication).

## 2026-11-21 MQTT 5 delivery quota at active connection capacity

The independent peer fills the configured MQTT 5 connection cohort
and checks refusal of an excess connection. One subscriber advertises
Receive Maximum one, reads the first QoS 2 delivery and holds PUBREC.
The publisher fills that subscriber's 256-delivery quota and verifies
PUBREC 0x97 twice. Idle peers answer PING while the quota remains full.
A disjoint topic completes 256 healthy QoS 2 exchanges before, during
and after the hold. The slow subscriber drains in payload order and
receives a new message using the rejected publisher packet ID. After
one idle client retires, a replacement connects and answers PING.

Both Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL completed five single-header repetitions
at 100 and 1,000 connections. The 20 runs checked 20 excess connection
refusals, 40 quota responses, 15,360 healthy exchanges and 5,140
deliveries through the slow subscriber. The 1,000-connection healthy
P99 medians were 306.4, 258.0 and 279.7 us on Windows, and 519.6,
433.8 and 401.6 us on WSL, before, during and after the hold. These
are serial exchange timings with the endurance runs active.

The modular server and codec suites passed on both environments.
The modular broker also passed the peer probe at 64 and 1,000
connections on both. WSL used ASan/UBSan with leak detection. The
existing dual-version standalone peer, generated-header freshness,
public API coverage and ordinary maturity passed. CI now invokes
the 64-connection case. Native Linux qualification and the 39
developing module declarations remain open.

## 2026-11-21 XRT TCP rearm after short epoll reads

The xredis socket trace located a speculative receive in XRT's
readiness loop. On an ordinary epoll read event, a successful short
read now rearms the existing level-triggered one-shot watch after
publishing the bytes. Full reads still drive the bounded loop. Read
events with hangup or error retain the terminal processing path.
The optimization applies to the epoll backend.
[Linux epoll semantics](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/epoll.7.html).

The rearm regression holds the first read callback after one byte.
The peer queues the remaining payload and FIN while the worker is
held. The test checks the remaining bytes are readable before releasing
the worker, then verifies ordered delivery, EOF and stream retirement.
It passed 25 times under WSL ASan/UBSan with leak detection. Returning
without rearming in an isolated negative build failed at the expected
EOF wait. The modular TCP and TCP Future suites passed on Windows
and WSL. Rebuilt MQTT broker examples also passed the ordinary
dual-version probe and five 1,000-connection pressure runs each.
The pressure probe now recognizes a refusal reset during connect.

The matched WSL comparison used the original XRT at `c0ae848d`
and the regenerated candidate. It verified all 400,000 replies across
30 runs using four RESP3 connections, 1,024-byte mixed GET/SET values,
a 128-slot window and two seconds per run. The Redis fixture used
logical CPU 6 and both client arms used CPUs 8 and 10. The trace used
Linux-local temporary storage.

| Traced at 2,000 offers/s | Baseline median | Candidate median |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| TCP send calls | 4,009 | 4,009 |
| TCP receive calls | 6,719 | 3,926 |
| Receive EAGAIN | 3,159 | 4 |
| TCP epoll registrations and removals, each | 3,163 | 3,858 |
| epoll wait calls | 837 | 1,285 |
| Send, receive, TCP epoll control and epoll wait combined | 17,897 | 16,933 |

The combined row is the median of per-run totals and fell 5.4%.
The untraced throughput medians matched the offered rates. At 2,000
and 12,000 offers/s the untraced P99 medians were 292.4 / 272.8 us
and 573.8 / 556.6 us in baseline / candidate order. The 12,000-rate
process CPU median was 2.963 / 3.046 seconds. All four untraced P99
series exceeded the variation gates. Native Linux release performance
remains open.

The source snapshots, binaries, modular and sanitizer logs, socket
traces, Redis counter checks and audit are under
`out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xredis-epoll-short-read/`.

The independent TCP peer now holds up to 10,000 MQTT 5 connections.

holds its 256-delivery quota. The observer checks PING in groups of
at most 128 sockets. It verifies a quota rejection before and after
replacement, then drains the slow subscriber and reuses the rejected
packet ID.

The initial immediate-replacement probe encountered TCP resets in
three WSL runs. The 1,000-connection run had completed eight
replacements. The two 10,000-connection runs had completed 44 and
80. The broker holds a connection slot until its native owner and
subscriptions retire. The probe allows retries of TCP refusal or
negative CONNACK within a five-second retry window and records the
counts. A reset after a successful CONNACK fails the test. A scripted
refusal exercised the retry and another injected failure verified the
partial JSON report and nonzero exit status.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu/WSL each passed three final 10,000-connection
runs. The six runs verified 60,000 initial connections, 600
replacements, 4,608 healthy QoS 2 exchanges and 1,542 deliveries
through the slow subscriber. The longest replacement through PING
was 23.138 ms on Windows and 0.886 ms on WSL. The final matrix saw
zero replacement refusals. The 5-, 64- and 1,000-connection smokes
and ordinary dual-version peer also passed on both environments.

The previous epoll rearm build passed all 93 WSL xredis test entries
and the modular MQTT dual-version server suite. The full WSL
checkpoint peer hit a timeout in its saturated APP writer fixture.
An isolated comparison reproduced that timeout in three of five

## 2026-11-21 MQTT checkpoint recovery across TCP, TLS and WebSocket

The combined APP examples build can select TCP, TLS, WS or WSS for
the checkpoint listener. It uses the shared listener, TLS credential
loader and WebSocket Upgrade code. All four transports use the same
checkpoint format and transaction callbacks.

The independent peer establishes a session and records its first
deliveries over WS or WSS, then recovers session presence, the
original QoS 1 DUP and QoS 2 PUBREL packet IDs and offline delivery
over TLS. It completes those exchanges, advances another outgoing
QoS 2 delivery and stops the broker while both TLS connections are
open. The saved image contains exactly one keyed outbound PUBREL.
The other WebSocket transport restores that PUBREL and verifies the
retained binary value. A final TCP connection verifies that the
completed deliveries have retired.
[MQTT 5.0 session retry rules](https://docs.oasis-open.org/mqtt/mqtt/v5.0/os/mqtt-v5.0-os.html).

The first pilot began with unkeyed deliveries from a plain snapshot
and observed the old QoS 1 delivery again after a process stop. The
existing store contract accepts unkeyed records with older callbacks.
The final probe enables online transactions before admitting its
first durable delivery.

The final matrix passed 24 transport paths across Windows x64 and
Ubuntu/WSL modular and single-header builds. Two additional paths
passed with WSL ASan/UBSan and leak detection during normal exits.
The combined example passed the full default TCP checkpoint peer
on both environments. Each host also verified that invalid credentials
and a transport request against the TCP-only build preserve the
existing image. Generated headers, API docs and ordinary maturity
passed. Strict release still lists 39 developing modules.

## 2026-11-21 xrpc TCP backpressure and reset isolation

The independent peer now drives two TCP connections through a single XRT executor worker in both duplex and direct-dispatch modes. It leaves 3,000-byte echo payloads unread, waits for a full send window and checks that a reply is queued. The healthy peer completes 128 ordered replies. The driver confirms backpressure again, resets the slow peer and verifies 128 further replies and clean output EOF on the healthy peer. The APP returns its expected peer-fault exit after retiring both owners and the pool.

The initial Windows probe accepted a single oversized send in full. The WSL send window became writable again before the reset check. The revised driver writes bounded chunks and fills the window again before reset. Native Windows and Ubuntu WSL each passed three full peer runs and the stdio peer. WSL ASan/UBSan with leak detection passed a seventh TCP run. Across the two modes this verified 14 backpressure and reset scenarios and 3,584 healthy replies. The test belongs to the existing Ubuntu TCP example step.

Generated single headers and the ordinary maturity audit passed. Strict release still reports `xrpc` and `xrpc_duplex` as developing. Native Linux and repeatable performance-tail acceptance remain open. Reports, component hashes and the first failed fixture are under `out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xrpc-tcp-backpressure/`.

## 2026-11-21 xcron restart catch-up after forced process termination

The independent restart peer terminates a live APP replay after reading two action records. It checks the complete emitted prefix and reopens the checkpoint from disk. The committed timestamp must equal the final observed occurrence or trail it by exactly one second. A new process runs the next two occurrences and persists progress within its supplied budget.

Windows x64 and Ubuntu WSL x64 each passed five complete restart-peer runs and the xcron test aggregate. In 8 of 10 interruptions the last emitted action was still uncommitted (5 Windows, 3 WSL). Each of those actions was replayed. The other 2 runs resumed after the last emitted action, which had committed before termination. All runs resumed from the recovered checkpoint and left the next backlog entry pending. The older simulated task failure, checkpoint write refusal and rollback cases still passed.

The ordinary maturity and single-header checks passed. Strict release still reports `xcron` and `xcron_scheduler` as developing. Native Linux, release-tail and power-loss acceptance remain open. Raw reports and build identities are under `out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xcron-process-interrupt/`.

## 2026-11-21 xredis interrupted pipeline across Redis restart

The restart driver waits for a completed binary ECHO on the observed Tracking connection, a blocked BLPOP and a full INCR frame queued behind it. The independent Redis 8.0.5 observer recorded two blocked clients and 48 bytes of queued input on the Tracking connection. The observer confirmed that INCR was absent from the old server's executed-command counters. The probe retains the reply and both pending Futures across process replacement and engine destruction. The completed reply keeps its payload and receive sequence. Both pending results report `DISCONNECTED` and `MAY_HAVE_EXECUTED` with no reply sequence. The replacement Redis ledger confirms no replay of the interrupted commands.

All ten trials passed. The native Windows and Ubuntu WSL clients each ran plaintext and TLS 1.3 with and without APP edits to the subscription intent. WSL ASan/UBSan with leak detection passed an additional plaintext and TLS trial. Redis ran in Ubuntu WSL for every trial, with the Windows client reaching it through loopback forwarding. The probe still validates restored pool and subscriber generations, a fresh Tracking connection, 16 recovered binary replies and full connection retirement. TLS also checked the untrusted certificate barrier. The first fixture used the synchronous Tracking entry point and waited behind its own blocking request. The passing fixture submits through the asynchronous entry point.

The generated single-header and ordinary maturity checks passed. Strict release still reports 29 developing modules. Native Linux, repeatable release tails and 72-hour qualification remain open. The run ledgers and the initial fixture failures are under `out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xredis-interrupted-pipeline/`.

The fixed-arrival observer ran one MQTT 5 publisher and eight wildcard subscribers with 128-byte payloads over plaintext TCP. Both reliable windows were 16. The two xmqtt engine workers and Mosquitto 2.1.2 used logical CPUs 0, 2, 4 and 6. The observer used 8 and 10. ## 2026-11-21 xcron APP registration through Wake

The new `wake_registration` example shows the single-owner API with an APP control thread. The first Wake requests registration. The owner registers the task and runs its callback. The callback notifies the control thread, which sends a shutdown Wake. The owner removes the task and joins the control thread before destroying the scheduler. The APP example uses the thread dependency already present in the examples aggregate.

The scheduler regression sends two signals before any native waiter exists. The first positive wait observes a single wake, and the next empty timed wait expires. Native Windows and Ubuntu WSL passed the modular and single-header suites and five fresh runs of the new APP on each platform. The WSL ASan/UBSan run with leak checking verified a further APP run. Standalone scheduler builds and generated assets passed. Strict release reports `xcron` and `xcron_scheduler` as developing. Native Linux and repeatable release tails remain open.

The module manifests, executable identities and per-process logs are under `out/service-extensions/scope-reduction-20261119/xcron-owner-wake/`. [Example guide](../../extlibs/xcron/examples/README.md).

## 2026-11-21 xredis RESP scalar line scan budget

The reader limits both delimiter searches to the remaining line budget. On
the following state-machine step, CRLF stays valid at exactly the limit.
A bare LF reports a protocol error, and an additional content byte reports
the line limit at that same offset. The fixture also checks retained input
after one frame and CRLF split by the feed budget.

and Ubuntu WSL. ASan/UBSan with leak detection passed the modular and

edits. The initial local Redis build lacked OpenSSL development headers.
The successful retry extracted the matching Ubuntu package into its build
directory. The generated single header and ordinary maturity check passed.
The strict xredis audit still reports 29 developing modules.

Seven alternating, single-CPU pairs compared the reader with 672040bc. A
